tasks.title: Define task-tree TDD/proof gate model
tasks.description:
Define the shared task-tree proof model that all Polaris workflow skills will use before any implementation-bearing step runs. The goal is broader than adding TDD to /start-build and /ship-task: every workflow step must require appropriate proof, while only implementation steps require the full red/green/refactor TDD loop.

Core model:
- Workflow entry gate before the task tree starts: task has a plan, dependencies are checked, testability path is known, and the first proof unit is identified.
- Proof unit shape: expected behavior -> proof before implementation -> observe failure or record explicit waiver -> implement smallest change -> observe passing proof -> proceed.
- Proof types: automated failing test, failing smoke command, failing API check, failing UI/browser check, registry diff expectation, manual verification script, review evidence, or explicit waiver that says no automated proof is possible and why.
- State behavior: if proof is missing or fails, stop the workflow and keep/revert the task to the previous valid lifecycle state instead of proceeding on inherited authority.
- Distinguish step roles: planning skills define proof; build skills execute proof; audit/review/promotion skills verify the proof trail.

Implementation notes:
1. Write the canonical definitions directly into the relevant command docs, starting with /plan-task, /start-build, /ship-task, /finish-build, /cross-boundary-audit, /review-pr, /codex-review, and /promote-stage.
2. Use consistent vocabulary: proof unit, entry evidence, exit evidence, waiver, proof trail, previous valid lifecycle state.
3. Decide where the proof trail is persisted: task plan in docs/backlog.json, Obsidian task tracker, PR body, or a combination. Prefer keeping summary evidence in backlog/Obsidian and detailed evidence in PR/session output.
4. Verification: run a dry task-tree walkthrough and confirm every step can say what proof it expects, where proof is recorded, and what happens when proof is missing.

## Design Discussion

Current workflow forces small tasks through an unnecessarily cumbersome planning process (/plan-task), creating friction and slowing delivery. Conversely, large tasks skip planning/breakdown entirely, leading to unfocused, noisy code that's error-prone and hard to manage. The impact field enables right-sizing the process to match task complexity: lightweight tasks get a fast path, complex tasks get decomposition guidance upfront.

## Outline Plan

Five phases: (1) Schema & Server Foundation â€” update backlog.json and server.js handlers to accept impact. (2) Backlog UI â€” Modals â€” add impact dropdown to Add and Edit modals. (3) Backlog UI â€” Table Display â€” add IMPACT column with color coding. (4) Integration & Refresh â€” ensure refresh preserves impact state. (5) Verification & Testing â€” end-to-end manual smoke test.

Phase 1 must complete before Phases 2â€“3 (UI depends on server). Phases 2â€“3 can run in parallel. Phase 4 depends on 2â€“3. Phase 5 is the final gate.

tasks.plan:
## Overview

server.js is a monolithic module handling config, secrets, WebSockets, agent loops, tool execution, MCP, backlog, evals, Cross-Check, file serving, and orchestration. As features grow, the monolith becomes harder to test, debug, and maintain. This refactoring extracts 8 bounded modules with explicit dependencies and a WebSocket adapter pattern to improve stability and maintainability.

## Architecture

Eight bounded modules will be created:
- contracts.ts: Type definitions and schemas (single source of truth)
- sessionStore.ts: Session state management and persistence
- agentRuntime.ts: Agent spawning and session loops
- toolRuntime.ts: Tool execution and schema validation
- mcpGateway.ts: MCP bridge and tool envelope handling
- crossCheck.ts: Cross-Check approval/rejection logic
- backlog.ts: Task operations and transitions
- httpRoutes.ts: HTTP endpoint routing and file serving

WebSocket server becomes a thin adapter over typed core operations: launchSession, executeTool, transitionTask, recordCrossCheck, loadMemory.

## Key Risks & Mitigations

Risk: Mission-critical code breakage. server.js is the engine of the entire player system.
Mitigation: Incremental extraction with rollback gates. Clear commit boundaries. Smoke tests after each phase.

Risk: Type boundary mismatch. Contracts module must capture all message shapes.
Mitigation: Audit server.js before extraction. Automated schema validation in WebSocket adapter.

Risk: Circular dependencies. Modules may accidentally depend on each other.
Mitigation: Contracts is a leaf. Core services depend only on contracts. WebSocket is a hub.

## Phases

1. Foundation: Extract contracts module
2. Core Services: Extract sessionStore, agentRuntime
3. Core Services: Extract toolRuntime, mcpGateway
4. Core Services: Extract crossCheck, backlog
5. HTTP Routes: Extract httpRoutes
6. WebSocket Adapter: Refactor websocket.ts as thin adapter
7. Integration: Wire modules, test, verify rollback
8. Documentation: Update Architecture.md, JSDoc, topology diagram

## First Proof Unit

Contracts module defined and compiles. All TypeScript types for WebSocket messages, tool contracts, and task orchestration are in src/runtime/contracts.ts and compile without errors.
